notes.meaning: Jerusalem was once packed with people and ruled over neighboring lands, but now she sits deserted and broken. She is pictured as a grieving widow who has lost her king and protector. Instead of reigning like an honored queen, she has been forced into bitter servitude as a captive.

Jerusalem weeps bitterly through the dark night when others are resting, and tears continually cover her cheeks. The foreign allies she once trusted and courted have completely abandoned her in her time of need. Instead of offering comfort, those former friends turned against her and became her open enemies.

The people of Judah have been dragged into exile and forced into harsh slavery. They are scattered among foreign nations and cannot find a single place of peaceful rest. When they tried to flee, their pursuers trapped them in tight spots where escape was impossible.

The roads leading up to Zion are pictured as mourning because pilgrims no longer travel them for the sacred feast days. The city gates stand empty and silent with no elders gathering to govern. Temple priests groan because worship has ceased, and the young women who once sang at holy celebrations are filled with deep anguish.

Jerusalem's enemies have become her masters and now live easily and securely. This disaster did not happen by accident; the Lord Himself brought this grief because the people repeatedly broke His laws. Even small children have been marched away into captivity before the eyes of their conquerors.

All the royal splendor and honor have completely stripped away from the city. Her leaders are compared to starving deer that cannot find any grass to eat. Lacking strength and courage from famine, they have no power left to outrun the hunters chasing them.

In the middle of her misery and wandering, Jerusalem looks back and remembers all the wonderful blessings she once took for granted. When her defenses collapsed, none of her former allies stepped forward to rescue her. Her conquerors simply stared at her ruins and mocked her fallen condition and silenced celebrations.

Jerusalem brought this terrible humiliation on herself by giving herself over to grievous rebellion against God. The neighboring nations that once respected her now view her with scorn because her moral weakness and guilt have been exposed for all to see. Feeling deeply disgraced, she can only groan and hide her face in shame.

Jerusalem's moral uncleanness was visible to everyone, sticking to her like dirt on the hem of a robe. She lived carelessly and never paused to think about where her sin would ultimately lead. Her sudden collapse was shocking to all, and in her total isolation she begs the Lord to notice how her enemies boast over her.

The Babylonian invaders seized all the cherished treasures of both the city and the temple. Most heartbreaking of all, pagan soldiers trampled right into the inner sacred rooms where God had forbidden foreigners even to set foot. The sight of God's holy house being plundered and profaned caused the deepest grief.

The surviving people groan with hunger as they wander about begging for something to eat. Families sold off their finest jewels and precious belongings just to buy enough bread to keep from fainting. In her deep distress, Jerusalem cries out to the Lord, pleading with Him to see how worthless and despised she has become.

Jerusalem calls out to travelers walking along the road, asking if they even care about her overwhelming pain. She invites everyone to stop and see whether any heartbreak on earth matches the agony inflicted upon her. She acknowledges that this crushing blow came directly from the Lord on the day of His righteous anger.

God's judgment felt like a burning fever sent from above, consuming her strength all the way into her bones. He acted like a hunter spreading a net to snare her feet, blocking every route of escape. He left her completely ruined, fainting, and sick at heart all day long.

Jerusalem's many sins were woven together into a heavy wooden yoke by God's own hand and strapped tightly onto her neck. This heavy burden of guilt drained all her strength and made her stumble. The Lord handed her over to enemies so mighty that she had no power to stand up against them.

The Lord cast down all the valiant soldiers who protected the city, leaving them powerless right inside the walls. He summoned the Babylonian army like a crowd gathering for a feast, but their purpose was to crush her young warriors. God trampled Jerusalem underfoot, crushing her like grapes being stomped in a winepress until the juice pours out.

Tears flow continuously like rivers because the city's sorrow is beyond words. The bitterest part of the pain is that God, the only true Comforter who could revive her fainting soul, feels far away. Her children are left defenseless and ruined because the enemy has completely conquered them.

Zion reaches out her hands desperately begging for aid, but finds no one to comfort her. The Lord Himself decreed that neighboring nations should surround Jacob and act as cruel enemies. Those surrounding nations now treat Jerusalem as something morally unclean and offensive, shunning her completely.

Even in her deep misery, Jerusalem confesses that the Lord is entirely fair and righteous in what He has done. She admits that she brought this punishment upon herself by rebelling against His clear words spoken through the prophets. She asks all the watching nations to notice her grief, especially as her young men and women are led off into captivity.

Jerusalem called out to her political allies for help, but they broke their promises and betrayed her. Inside the besieged city, even the respected priests and civic leaders starved to death. Their high rank could not protect them as they desperately searched for small bits of bread just to stay alive.

Jerusalem cries directly to the Lord, describing the churning in her stomach and the heavy pounding of her troubled heart. She honestly confesses that this agony came because of her stubborn rebellion against Him. Out in the open streets the sword kills her people, while inside the homes famine and sickness bring deadly silence.

People hear Jerusalem's painful groaning, but no human comforter steps in to help. Her enemies know all about her disaster, and they rejoice because they see that the Lord Himself brought this judgment upon her. She pleads with God to bring the day of justice He promised, so that those proud, mocking nations will experience the same accountability she had to face.

Jerusalem asks God to bring all the cruel deeds of her enemies before His judgment seat and deal with them fairly. She does not claim to be innocent, openly confessing that her own disaster came because of her many sins. She closes her prayer by laying her endless groans and faint, weary heart before the mercy of God.
